Hazael
HAZ-ay-el
proper noun (a king of Syria)
Hebrew Chaza'el, “God has seen,” from chazah (to see) and El (God); the Syrian who murdered his master to seize the throne of Damascus.

📖 Biblical Definition

Hazael was a servant of Ben-hadad king of Syria whom the LORD marked out, through Elijah and afterward Elisha, to be the rod of His chastisement upon faithless Israel. When the Lord at Horeb commissioned Elijah, He named Hazael to be anointed king over Syria, an instrument of judgment alongside Jehu and Elisha. The dreadful scene of his rise is recorded when sick Ben-hadad sent him to inquire of Elisha whether he should recover. The prophet fixed his countenance upon Hazael until he was ashamed, and the man of God wept, for he foresaw the evil Hazael would do to the children of Israel: their strong holds set on fire, their young men slain, their children dashed, their women with child ripped up. Hazael, feigning humility, protested, “Is thy servant a dog, that he should do this great thing?” yet the next day he smothered his master with a wet cloth and reigned in his stead. Thereafter the LORD began to cut Israel short, and Hazael oppressed them all the days of Jehoahaz. Hazael is the dictionary's standing case that God ordains even the wicked as the instruments of His righteous judgment without being the author of their sin—the murderer is fully guilty, and yet the sword he wields is the sword the LORD appointed against a covenant people who would not repent.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The Syrian servant who murdered Ben-hadad and seized the throne of Damascus, foreseen by Elisha as the LORD's rod of judgment upon apostate Israel; a study in God's sovereign use of a guilty instrument.

expand to see more

HAZAEL, proper noun. [Hebrew, God has seen.] A servant of Ben-hadad king of Syria, afterward king of Damascus.

Elijah was charged at Horeb to anoint him king over Syria, one of three instruments of judgment upon Israel.

Sent to Elisha concerning his master's sickness, he heard the prophet foretell the evil he would work upon Israel, and Elisha wept.

He murdered Ben-hadad with a wet cloth and reigned in his stead, then oppressed Israel all his days.

An example of a wicked man whom God ordains as the rod of His chastisement, guilty in his sin yet serving the divine purpose.

📖 Key Scripture

1 Ki 19:15 — "And the LORD said unto him, Go, return on thy way to the wilderness of Damascus: and when thou comest, anoint Hazael to be king over Syria."

2 Ki 8:12 — "And Hazael said, Why weepeth my lord? And he answered, Because I know the evil that thou wilt do unto the children of Israel: their strong holds wilt thou set on fire, and their young men wilt thou slay with the sword, and wilt dash their children, and rip up their women with child."

2 Ki 8:13 — "And Hazael said, But what, is thy servant a dog, that he should do this great thing? And Elisha answered, The LORD hath shewed me that thou shalt be king over Syria."

2 Ki 10:32 — "In those days the LORD began to cut Israel short: and Hazael smote them in all the coasts of Israel."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is the squeamish refusal to confess that God sovereignly ordains wicked instruments of judgment while holding them wholly guilty.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the hard, comforting doctrine of providence over the wicked. The modern mind recoils from a God who names a murderer beforehand and weeps not over the LORD's decree but over the sin of the man. Yet Scripture holds both without flinching: the LORD appointed Hazael as His rod (1 Kings 19:15), and Hazael is fully guilty of the blood he shed. God is not the author of sin; He ordains its bounds and bends even the cruelty of nations to the chastening of His people.

Hazael also exposes the deceit of the human heart. “Is thy servant a dog, that he should do this great thing?” he asked, certain he could never sink so low—and committed the murder within a day. The man who cannot imagine himself capable of a sin is the man nearest to it. The dictionary names this as the total depravity the confession teaches: not that every man is as wicked as he could be, but that no chamber of the heart is exempt, and self-trust is the surest road to the crime one swore one would never commit.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Hebrew chazah (to see, to behold in vision) and El (God), “God has seen”—a name of irony over a man whose deeds God saw and judged.

expand to see more

Chaza'el, Hebrew, “God has seen,” from chazah, to see or behold.

El, the general Semitic name for God, here joined to the verb of seeing.

Ben-hadad, “son of Hadad,” the dynastic name of the Syrian kings he served and slew.

The “rod” imagery of Isaiah 10:5 illumines Hazael's office: the heathen power as the staff of God's indignation.

The wet cloth (Hebrew makber, a coverlet) is the homely instrument of the regicide recorded in 2 Kings 8:15.

Usage

"The elder cited Hazael to show that God may ordain a wicked nation as His rod without ever being the author of its cruelty."

"“Is thy servant a dog?” the preacher quoted, then warned that the heart most sure it cannot fall is the heart nearest the fall."

"She trembled to read that Elisha wept, not over God's decree, but over the evil a man would freely choose."
